title: About
text:
I am an Associate Professor of Economics at the Norris-Vincent College of Business at Angelo State University and a Research Assistant Professor at the Free Market Institute at Texas Tech University. I hold a Ph.D. from the Department of Agricultural and Applied Economics at Texas Tech University.
My research combines ethnographic fieldwork and case studies with quantitative approaches — including natural experiments — to examine how formal and informal institutions interact to shape economic and political outcomes. I work primarily on low- and middle-income countries, with a focus on Latin America.

title: About
text:
Andes Libres
Before graduate school, I founded and directed Andes Libres, an educational think tank based in Cusco, Peru. The organization offered university students, rural communities, and local entrepreneurs access to economics and public policy research through forums, conferences, and debates. It also provided business training and connected participants with scholarly networks across Peruvian universities.

title: Research
text:
“Friends or Foes? The Insurgent’s Dilemma of Seeking Legitimacy While Keeping Secrets”
World Development, 2026
SSRN

Why do some rebel groups court public legitimacy while others stay hidden? I model the trade-off insurgents face between openness — which wins popular support, resources, and civilian collaboration — and secrecy, which shields the group from being targeted. The theory is tested against Peru’s Shining Path and Túpac Amaru movements (1980–2000).



“A Self-Defense Network against Terrorism and Crime: Evidence from Peru”
Terrorism and Political Violence, 2023
Published version

Self-governance is often assumed not to scale beyond small groups. Yet hundreds of thousands of Peruvian peasants built a decentralized, multi-community network of patrols (rondas campesinas) that provided security with no central direction — a polycentric order that played a decisive role in defeating crime and terrorism between 1980 and 2000.



“The Influence of Pinochet in the Chilean Miracle”
Latin American Research Review, 2022
Published version

Using a synthetic-control counterfactual, I find that Chilean income per capita underperformed comparable countries for at least fifteen years after Pinochet’s coup, and that the growth of 1985–1997 did not depend on his autocracy — challenging the popular narrative that credits the dictatorship with Chile’s economic “miracle.”



“Night Watchers and Terrorists”
Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, 2020
Published version

The peasant self-defense patrols that arose to fight the Shining Path adopted strikingly different internal structures — democratic in the north, hierarchical in the south. I develop an organizational theory showing how the severity and time horizon of the external threat shaped whether these extralegal groups organized horizontally or vertically.



“Fighting on Christmas: Brawling as Self-Governance in Rural Peru”
with Raymond March
Journal of Institutional Economics, 2020
Published version

The Andean Christmas ritual of Takanakuy — public, consensual brawling — works as a community mechanism for resolving disputes that Peru’s formal courts cannot or will not settle, sustaining cooperation and social order through locally accepted rules.

title: Research
text:
Book Chapters

“Por la Razón o la Fuerza: What Caused Chile’s Economic Miracle?”
in The Pinochet Shock: Radical Change and Life Under Dictatorship, Palgrave Macmillan, 2025
Chapter


A chapter revisiting the sources of Chile’s economic transformation and asking how much of the country’s growth can be attributed to the Pinochet regime versus the market reforms of the period.



“A Government Role Conducive to Liberty: Operation Warp Speed”
with Peter C. Earle
in Pandemics and Liberty, American Institute for Economic Research, 2022
Book


A chapter examining Operation Warp Speed — the U.S. effort to accelerate COVID-19 vaccine development — as a case of a limited government role that can remain compatible with individual liberty.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers

“Resource Shocks and Local Regulatory Capacity: Evidence from Peru”


Examines how windfalls in natural-resource revenue affect the regulatory capacity of local governments in Peru.



“Co-Producing the State: Formal Recognition of Extralegal Governance and Fiscal Capacity”


Studies how the state’s formal recognition of pre-existing extralegal (community) governance shapes its fiscal capacity, drawing on evidence from Peru.

title: Enrique Escalante
text:
I am an Associate Professor of Economics at the Norris-Vincent College of Business at Angelo State University and a Research Assistant Professor at the Free Market Institute at Texas Tech University.
My research lies at the intersection of political economy and institutional economics. I study how informal governance, political violence, and state capacity shape economic and social outcomes, with a focus on Latin America. A second research stream examines the long-run effects of welfare state expansion on family structure in the United States.
